SUBSECTION.NAME: Running the Evaluator as a Program
SUBSECTION.TEXT:
Given the evaluator, we have in our hands a description
(expressed in Lisp) (expressed in Python)
of the process by which
Lisp expressions Python statements and expressions
are evaluated. One advantage of expressing the evaluator as a program is that we can run the program. This gives us, running within
Lisp, Python,
a working model of how
Lisp Python
itself evaluates expressions. This can serve as a framework for experimenting with evaluation rules, as we shall do later in this chapter.

Our evaluator program reduces expressions ultimately to the application of

There must be a binding for each built-in

of an application of a built-in function, it will find an object to pass to apply. We thus set up a metacircular evaluator for Pythonglobal environment global environmentmetacircularin metacircular evaluator

procedures functions and operators
that can appear in the expressions we will be evaluating. symbol(s)in global environment
The global environment also includes bindings for the symbols metacircular evaluator for Schemetrue and falsetrue and false true and false, so that they can be used as constants in expressions to be evaluated.
The built-in environment also includes bindings for predefined constants such as metacircular evaluator for Pythonmath_pimath_pi math_pi. The environment in which the program is evaluated is the global environment, which is the built-in environment extended by a frame that is initially empty. As we saw in section, assignments and function definitions at the top level of the program add their names to this frame.

Apply-in-underlying-scheme is the apply procedure we have used in earlier chapters. The metacircular evaluators apply procedure (section) models the working of this primitive. Having two different things called apply leads to a technical problem in running the metacircular evaluator, because defining the metacircular evaluators apply will mask the definition of the primitive. One way around this is to rename the metacircular apply to avoid conflict with the name of the primitive procedure. We have assumed instead that we have saved a reference to the underlying apply by doing
apply_in_underlying
(define apply-in-underlying-scheme apply)
before defining the metacircular apply. This allows us to access the original version of apply under a different name.
The function apply_in_underlying_python apply_in_underlying_python is a built-in function of the language that applies a given function to the elements of a given linked list, which serve as the arguments. We also made use of apply_in_underlying_python to define the function apply_generic in section.
apply_built_in_function apply_primitive_procedure apply_primitive_procedure_example 3

def apply_built_in_function(fun, arglist): return apply_in_underlying_python(built_in_implementation(fun), arglist)

For convenience in running the metacircular evaluator, we provide a metacircular evaluator for Schemedriver loop driver loopmetacircularin metacircular evaluator driver loop that models the read-eval-print loop of the underlying Lisp system. It prints a prompts prompt, reads an input expression, evaluates this expression in the global environment, and prints the result. We precede each printed result by an output prompt so as to distinguish the value of the expression from other output that may be printed.The primitive procedure read primitive proceduresfunctions (those marked ns are not in the IEEE Scheme standard)readread read waits for input from the user, and returns the next complete expression that is typed. For example, if the user types (+ 23 x), read returns a three-element list containing the symbol +, the number 23, and the symbol x. ' (single quote)readread and quotereadread and If the user types 'x, read returns a two-element list containing the symbol quote and the symbol x.

For convenience in running the metacircular evaluator, we provide a metacircular evaluator for Pythondriver loop driver loopmetacircularin metacircular evaluator driver loop that repeatedly reads and evaluates programs. It prints a prompts promptsmetacircular evaluator prompt and reads an input program as a string. It transforms the program string into a tagged-linked-list representation of the statement as described in sectiona process called parsing and accomplished by the built-in function parse. As when Python runs a program, the only output is what the program prints. The driver loop gets the global environment as argument and evaluates each program with respect to it. Names that the program assigns or defines are added to the global environment and are thus available to the programs that are read in later iterations of the driver loop.
